nvitk.gui.panels.statmodels¶

Statmodels explorer — interactive mixed-effects and mediation modeling over the NVITK DB.

Description¶

Split into focused modules; import StatmodelsPanel / StatmodelsWindow from here.

constants static choices and defaults theme dark palette, stylesheet, and the white-figure helper helpers repo access, formula parsing, checklist utilities frame_table analysis dataframe with column-anchored filtering derived derived-column editor (log, z-score, expressions) measurements multi-measurement selection and background frame loading report model info: stat chips over tabbed tables plot_view canvas, group include/exclude checklist, axis sliders mediation_panel mediation form and its worker window the explorer window itself panel the right-tab launcher

Side by side rather than stacked — stacking them made the controls row about twice as tall as it needed to be, and every pixel there comes straight out of the figure.

_build_map_options() → qtpy.QtWidgets.QWidget¶

Second options row: the controls that belong to the anatomical maps.

Split off the general row because there are now a dozen of them, and mixing the two meant the map controls reflowed into whatever gap the general ones left — different position every time the analysis type changed. Its own row keeps them together and hides them as a group.

_on_frame_load_failed(message: str) → None¶

_recompute_frame(*, announce: bool = True) → None¶

Rebuild the working frame: derived columns first, then the filter rules.

Both stages always start from the untouched _analysis_df, so removing a filter or editing a derived column can never compound on a previously filtered frame. Derived columns come first because filters must be able to target them (log_pi > 0).

_sync_column_combos(df: pandas.DataFrame | None) → None¶

Repopulate the plot-x combo from df’s columns.

Kept explicit rather than folded into the table refresh: when it rode along with the old table population it silently stopped updating whenever the table was drawn from a different frame.

_sync_group_combo(df: pandas.DataFrame | None) → None¶

Repopulate the colour-by combo: random grouping factors, then categorical fixed effects.

A column is offered when it has at least two levels and few enough to draw — a 510-level subject factor is still listed (it is the model’s own grouping) but never preselected.

_on_edit_column_filter(column: str) → None¶

Open the per-column filter dialog and merge its rules into the active set.

_on_clear_column_filter(column: str) → None¶

Drop every rule anchored to column.

_on_quick_transform(column: str, transform: str) → None¶

Add a canned transform of column straight from the header menu.

_on_edit_combinations() → None¶

Open the region-combinations editor and re-apply the result.

Open the derived-columns editor, optionally on the bins page for bin_column.

_on_bin_column(column: str) → None¶

Open the derived-columns editor to cut column into labelled groups.

_hover_columns(df: pandas.DataFrame) → list[str]¶

Identifier and QC columns worth attaching to every point’s hover box.

static _panel_note(fig: Any) → str¶

How many anatomical panels a grouped figure ended up with.

The two backends record it differently: Matplotlib figures carry linked_axes, Plotly subplot figures carry a summary in layout.meta. Reading only one gave “0 panels” on the other.

_excluded_points(x: str, y: str, group: str) → pandas.DataFrame | None¶

The observations the active filters removed, in the columns the plot uses.

These are not in the model frame — the fit ran on the filtered data — so there is nothing inside it to grey out. They have to come from the unfiltered analysis frame and be drawn as a separate series, which is what makes it visible whether a filter took out a coherent cluster or scattered noise.

None when nothing was filtered, or when the plot’s columns are not all present in the analysis frame (a fit can rename them), since guessing a mapping would mislabel points.

_sync_filter_toggle() → None¶

Enable the grey-out toggle only when a filter has actually removed something.

_region_column_name() → str¶

Whichever column carries the vessel identity in this frame.

_to_wide(df: pandas.DataFrame) → pandas.DataFrame¶

Pivot a long frame to one row per subject and one column per vessel.

The cell value is the primary measurement; subject-level covariates ride along, so age_c and sex stay available to every structural equation. Per-vessel coverage is recorded in self._wide_coverage — with a dozen vessels in one model, listwise deletion is decided by whichever vessel is measured least often, and that is the number worth knowing before blaming the model.

Returns the frame unchanged, with a warning, when it cannot be pivoted: a failed reshape should not empty the table the user is looking at.

_sync_reshape_buttons(df: pandas.DataFrame | None) → None¶

Enable the reshape controls from the frame’s shape, not from which button was last pressed.

A frame loaded on the subject grain is already wide without the reshape button having been touched, so gating on _wide_mode left Melt disabled on exactly the frames it exists for.

_melt_working(df: pandas.DataFrame) → pandas.DataFrame¶

Melt self._melt_family’s per-region columns back to long, or return df unchanged.

_on_melt_frame() → None¶

Choose a measurement family to melt back into a territory column.

_coverage_note() → str¶

One line naming the vessels that decide listwise deletion, or "".

_on_reshape_frame() → None¶

Toggle the analysis dataframe between long and wide (one column per vessel).

_structural_columns() → set[str]¶

Columns the frame is built on, which dropping would break rather than simplify.

The subject key, the region key and the primary measurement are what every later stage addresses: filters join on them, the reshape pivots on them, and the measurement is the cell value. Removing one does not give a smaller frame, it gives a frame nothing can be rebuilt from.

_on_drop_column(column: str) → None¶

Hide a column from the working frame, leaving the dataset untouched.

_on_change_column_type(column: str, kind: str) → None¶

Recast one column, or clear its override with auto.

_on_set_reference_level(column: str, level: str) → None¶

Make level the treatment reference for column, or clear the override.

_on_restore_columns() → None¶

Put every dropped column back.

_on_export_summary(column: str, by: str) → None¶

Export per-group descriptive statistics for one measurement.

Summarises the working frame — derived columns computed, filters applied — so the table describes the rows a model would be fitted on rather than the raw load. The export carries a provenance sheet and the underlying values, because a sheet of means with no record of which column, which grouping and which confidence level is unreadable a month later.

_on_qc_filter(column: str, key: str) → None¶

Apply a ready-made quality-control filter to the analysis dataframe.

These drop rows, so they change the fit — unlike the plot’s QC gate, which only greys observations out. Existing rules on the same columns are replaced rather than stacked, so re-picking a preset re-applies it instead of intersecting two copies of itself.

_on_column_plot(column: str, kind: str) → None¶

Open the distribution viewer for one column.

Draws from the unfiltered frame with the filtered-out rows marked, so the plot shows what the filters removed rather than hiding it — which is the only way to tell a filter that took out a coherent cluster from one that took out scattered noise.

_on_subject_plot(subject: str) → None¶

Open the anatomical viewer for one subject.

Drawn from the working frame, unlike the column viewer: this window is about what a subject’s anatomy looks like, and painting a vessel the filters have already rejected would show a value the analysis is not using.

_frame_with_exclusions(base: pandas.DataFrame) → tuple[pandas.DataFrame, Any]¶

The derived frame plus a boolean mask of the rows the active filters removed.

The mask is built by comparing the filtered frame’s index against the unfiltered one, so it follows whatever rules are active without this needing to re-implement them.

_on_publish_column(column: str) → None¶

Write a derived column into the dataset as a variable.

The target table follows the column’s source: a transform of an image measurement becomes an image measurement keyed on subject × region, a transform of a clinical variable becomes a clinical one keyed on subject. The dialog states which and why, and nothing is written until it is confirmed — this is the one action here that changes a shared dataset.

_on_export_frame() → None¶

Save the active (derived + filtered) frame to a spreadsheet.

_on_set_plot_x(column: str) → None¶

Use column as the plot’s x axis.

_analysis_kind() → str¶

The selected analysis type.

_on_glm_family_changed() → None¶

Offer only the links the selected GLM family supports, and describe it.

_r_backend_status()¶

Probe the R backend once per window — the Rscript call takes a moment.

_on_formula_changed() → None¶

Keep the MMRM covariance controls in step with an inline term as it is typed.

_mmrm_backend_status()¶

Probe the mmrm backend once per window.

_robust_backend_status()¶

Probe the robustbase backend once per window.

_suggested_mmrm_term() → str¶

A covariance term that would suit the loaded frame, offered when the formula lacks one.

_sync_mmrm_hint() → None¶

Describe the covariance term written in the formula, and pre-flight it against the frame.

The term is part of the formula, so it is read from there rather than assembled from controls — but it still drives the checks that R’s own error messages do not make obvious: which columns it needs, whether any subject × level cell is duplicated, and whether the structure has more parameters than the data can support.

_on_convert_to_lme4() → None¶

Rewrite the MixedLM fields as a single lme4 formula, in place.

_on_insert_term() → None¶

Insert a spline / polynomial term into the formula at the cursor.

_on_insert_covariance_term() → None¶

Insert an mmrm covariance term into the formula at the cursor.

_sync_analysis_type() → None¶

Swap the formulation panel and hide the controls the selected engine does not use.

_sync_nonlinear_columns(df: pandas.DataFrame | None) → None¶

Offer the frame’s numeric columns as the curve’s x and y.

_on_fit() → None¶

Fit the selected model on the working frame, then show its report and plot.

_fit_formula_model(kind: str)¶

Fit MixedLM / OLS / GLM from the shared formulation panel.

_fit_nonlinear()¶

Fit the selected parametric curve of y against x.

_sync_plot_levels(df: pandas.DataFrame, column: str) → None¶

Rebuild the plot’s group checklist from column’s levels in df.

_covariate_reference_values(df: pandas.DataFrame, formula: str, exclude: set[str]) → dict[str, Any]¶

Reference value for every formula term the EMM grid does not already vary.

The grid patsy evaluates only carries the x axis and the facet column. Any other term in the formula — a second measurement, a covariate, another categorical factor — is simply absent, and patsy raises NameError for it, which used to leave the plot showing raw points and no model curves at all.

Numeric terms are pinned at their mean, categorical ones at their most frequent level. The marginal means are then read “at average age, for the modal group”, which is the usual EMM convention.

_on_plot() → None¶

Redraw the current analysis’s plot with the active display options.

_plot_mmrm() → None¶

Least-squares means by the repeated dimension, or the estimated correlation matrix.

The correlation heatmap is the one worth looking at for an unstructured fit: it shows whether the equal-correlation assumption a random-intercept model makes is anywhere near the truth.

_plot_lme4() → None¶

Population and per-group curves predicted through pymer4.

_plot_lmrob() → None¶

Robust fit curves, or the robustness weights.

The weights figure is the one specific to this engine: it shows which observations the estimator discounted, which is a QC shortlist rather than a result.

_on_insert_network_syntax() → None¶

Write the vascular path model into the formula box, built from the vessels present.

_sync_sem_groups() → None¶

Offer the frame’s low-cardinality factors as a multi-group split.

Continuous columns and identifiers are excluded: a multi-group fit estimates the whole model once per level, so grouping on subject_uid asks for one SEM per subject, each on a single row.

_plot_sem() → None¶

Path coefficients, the fitted diagram, the measurement model, or the misfit diagnostics.

_map_display() → str¶

Which anatomical map is selected — "vascular", "brain", or "" for neither.

Every place that used to compare the Display combo against the literal "vascular" asks this instead, so adding a third map is one entry in _MAP_DISPLAYS rather than a hunt through the gating.

_sync_map_contrasts(display: str) → None¶

Populate the contrast picker from the fit’s interaction terms, or hide it.

Discovery is anatomy-specific: an interaction term only counts if one of its factors names a level this map can draw. So the vascular map asks the vessel table and the brain map asks the atlas — using the vessel resolver for a cortical model finds no interaction at all and silently hides the picker, which is what made the brain map’s contrast views unreachable.

_vascular_plot_kinds() → tuple[tuple[str, str], Ellipsis]¶

Views the vascular map can offer for the current fit.

A model whose vessel information lives in a random term — (1 + age_c | territory) — has nothing about individual vessels in its fixed effects, so the coefficient view would fall back to observed means without saying why. When per-group terms exist they are offered first, one entry each, because they are what that model actually estimated per vessel.

_brain_plot_kinds() → tuple[tuple[str, str], Ellipsis]¶

Views the brain map can offer for the current fit.

Same rule as _vascular_plot_kinds(): a model whose parcel information lives in a random term has nothing about individual parcels in its fixed effects, so those terms are offered first rather than letting the coefficient view fall back to observed means without saying why.

_brain_atlas_key() → str¶

The atlas to draw on — the picker’s choice, or the one the plotted measurement was made under.

A measurement loaded under the vascular parcellation carries no Desikan parcels at all, so silently defaulting to Desikan there draws nothing and makes a configuration mismatch look like a modelling failure.

_plot_brain() → None¶

Draw the fit’s per-parcel numbers on the cortical surface.

_plot_vascular() → None¶

Draw the fit’s per-vessel numbers on the cerebral circulation schematic.

_plot_mrf() → None¶

The smoothed field over the vessels, or the adjacency graph it was smoothed on.

_plot_nonlinear() → None¶

Scatter plus the fitted curve, coloured by the grouping column when it is present.

_on_run_mediation(spec: nvitk.stats.mediation.MediationSpec) → None¶

Start a mediation run on the working frame.

_on_cancel_mediation() → None¶

Ask the running mediation to stop.

_on_mediation_done(bundle: dict[str, Any]) → None¶

Show the mediation report and its default plot.

_on_mediation_failed(message: str) → None¶

Report a failed mediation run.

_set_plot_kinds(choices: Sequence[tuple[str, str]]) → None¶

Repopulate the figure picker, preserving the current pick when it survives.

_sync_mediation_plot_choices(bundle: dict[str, Any]) → None¶

Offer only the figures this engine’s result can actually produce.

_plot_mediation() → None¶

Draw the selected mediation figure.

_config_dict() → dict[str, Any]¶

Serialize every panel setting to a plain dict (saved alongside a fitted model).

_apply_config(cfg: dict[str, Any], *, allow_expressions: bool = True) → None¶

Restore the panel from a saved config, migrating older schema versions first.

Parameters:

allow_expressions (bool) – When False, expression-kind derived columns are dropped instead of restored. Expressions are evaluated code, and a config file can come from anywhere the user browsed to — _on_load() decides whether the source is trusted.

_on_save() → None¶

Save the fitted model, its configuration and its report under nvitk-statmodels/<name>/.

The engines serialize very differently — a statsmodels result pickles, an lme4 or MMRM fit lives in R, a non-linear fit is a dict holding a closure — so the model artifact is written best-effort and last. The configuration, the report and the coefficient table are written regardless: losing the record of a fit because its object would not pickle is the worse outcome, and that is exactly what used to happen.

_sync_display_enabled() → None¶

Grey the Display picker out for figures that are not a family of curves.

MMRM offers both least-squares means, which panel, and a correlation heatmap, which is a single matrix with nothing to split — so the picker follows the figure choice there.

_on_export_plot() → None¶

Prompt for a location and write the displayed figure there as a PNG.

_save_model_artifact(out_dir: pathlib.Path) → str¶

Serialize the fitted model object itself, however this engine allows.

statsmodels results pickle. An lme4 or MMRM fit is an R object, so it goes to .rds — readable back in R with readRDS, which is more useful than a Python pickle would be. A non-linear fit holds a closure, so its parameters are written instead of the object.

Returns the file name written, and raises if the engine offers no route at all.

_on_load() → None¶

Prompt for a saved model directory and restore its config, model and summary.

_trusts_expressions(model_dir: pathlib.Path, cfg: dict[str, Any]) → bool¶

Decide whether to evaluate expression-kind derived columns from a loaded config.

Expressions are code. A config saved by this tool under the dataset’s own nvitk-statmodels/ directory is the user’s own work; one browsed to from anywhere else might not be, so ask before evaluating it.
